Getting started with latentmixtures

latentmixtures.Rmd

latentmixtures fits latent class, latent profile, latent transition and growth mixture models from R. You write ordinary R (data frames, pipes, tidyselect); the estimation runs in the Julia package LatentMixtures.jl, in one Julia process that persists for the whole R session. This vignette covers installation, the Julia session, latent class and latent profile analysis, class enumeration and tables. Two further vignettes cover longitudinal models (vignette("longitudinal")) and auxiliary variables, weights and multigroup models (vignette("auxiliary")); vignette("plotting") shows the figures.

All examples use the simulated datasets shipped with the package (?aces, ?wellbeing, ?wellbeing_panel, ?depression, ?substance). Because they were generated from known models, the estimates can be compared with the truth.

Installation

  1. Install Julia (>= 1.12), for example with juliaup. JuliaConnectoR must find the julia executable: put it on the PATH or set JULIA_BINDIR, for example in ~/.Renviron:

    JULIA_BINDIR=~/.juliaup/bin

  2. Install the R package and its R dependencies (JuliaConnectoR, rlang, tidyselect).

  3. Install the Julia package once, from a local copy or from its Git repository:

library(latentmixtures)
install_julia_packages(path = "path/to/LatentMixtures.jl")
# or install_julia_packages(url = "<Git URL of LatentMixtures.jl>")

lm_available() then returns TRUE. For GPU estimation, also install CUDA.jl into the same Julia environment.

The Julia session

Fitting functions start Julia automatically. Starting it yourself lets you choose the number of threads, which are used for random starts and bootstrap replications:

library(latentmixtures)
lm_start(threads = 4)
#> Starting Julia ...
#> Julia 1.12.5 started with 4 threads; LatentMixtures.jl loaded.
lm_status()
#> Julia 1.12.5 running: 4 threads, LatentMixtures.jl loaded (session 1)

The first fit of each model type in a session includes Julia’s compilation time; later fits are fast. The thread count of a running process cannot change: use lm_end(); lm_start(threads = n). Models fitted before lm_end() still print, but have to be refitted for anything that needs Julia (parameters, posteriors, auxiliary models).

Latent class analysis: patterns of childhood adversity

aces holds retrospective reports of eight adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) by 1,500 adults: emotional, physical and sexual abuse, emotional and physical neglect, witnessed domestic violence, household substance misuse and household mental illness, each coded 0/1 with 2% missing. The data were generated from four classes (Low adversity, Household dysfunction, Maltreatment, High adversity; shares 0.52, 0.20, 0.17, 0.11).

data(aces)
round(colMeans(aces[, 2:9], na.rm = TRUE), 3)   # prevalence of each ACE
#>    ace_emo_abuse   ace_phys_abuse    ace_sex_abuse  ace_emo_neglect 
#>            0.293            0.227            0.151            0.239 
#> ace_phys_neglect     ace_violence    ace_substance       ace_mental 
#>            0.132            0.228            0.283            0.261

Choose the indicators with tidyselect and the number of classes with K. starts mirrors Mplus STARTS; the default is 100 random starts of 20 EM iterations, the best 20 iterated to convergence.

m4 <- aces |> lca(starts_with("ace_"), K = 4)
convergence(m4)   # check that the best LL is replicated and EM reached the maximum
#> Convergence check: ✓ no problems found
#>   best start converged      yes (77 EM iterations)
#>   stage-2 starts converged  20 / 20
#>   best LL replicated        20 times
#>   LL at EM / after Newton   -5248.0073 / -5248.0073 (gain 0.0e+00; max |gradient| 1.4e-13)
#>   smallest class            0.099
#>   · EM converged; 1 Newton steps (polish = true) raised the log-likelihood by 5.5e-07 (max |gradient| 1.3e-03 → 3.3e-07); the reported solution is the Newton one
m4
#> ━━ Latent class analysis ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

The printout shows the fit statistics (log-likelihood, number of free parameters, AIC, BIC, sample-size adjusted BIC, entropy, smallest class and how often the best log-likelihood was replicated), the class sizes with average posterior probabilities, and the item-response probabilities. The four generating classes are recovered: a large low-adversity class, a maltreatment class (abuse and neglect), a household-dysfunction class (violence, substance misuse, mental illness) and a small class with high probabilities on everything. Missing responses are handled by full-information maximum likelihood; rows with every item missing are not analysed.

summary(m4)                    # every parameter with robust (MLR) standard errors

classify() returns one row per input row (with NA for rows that were not analysed), so it can be bound to the data:

post <- classify(m4)
aces2 <- cbind(aces, post[c("p1", "p2", "p3", "p4", "class")])
table(aces2$class)
#> 
#>   1   2   3   4 
#> 876 262 212 150

Indicators may be numeric codes, factors, characters or logicals; factor labels are used in the output. Raw survey or Mplus files often code missing values as -999; convert them before fitting:

raw <- read.table(system.file("extdata", "lca_bin.dat", package = "latentmixtures"))
raw[raw == -999] <- NA
colSums(is.na(raw))
#>  V1  V2  V3  V4  V5  V6  V7  V8 
#> 123 110 106 120 119 113 114 111

Latent profile analysis: health behaviours and wellbeing

lpa() takes continuous indicators. wellbeing has six of them for 1,000 adults: hours of sleep, hours of physical activity per week, servings of fruit and vegetables, stress (PSS-4), loneliness (UCLA-3) and life satisfaction. They were generated from four profiles (Thriving, Typical, Stressed short sleepers, Isolated and inactive) with profile-specific variances and modest within-profile correlations. variances and covariances choose the within-profile structure: equal variances with local independence (Mplus default), profile-specific variances, or full covariance matrices.

data(wellbeing)
p_eq <- wellbeing |> lpa(sleep:lifesat, K = 4)                        # equal variances
p_vv <- wellbeing |> lpa(sleep:lifesat, K = 4, variances = "varying") # profile-specific
p_full <- wellbeing |> lpa(sleep:lifesat, K = 4, variances = "varying", covariances = "varying")
convergence(p_vv)   # check that the best LL is replicated and EM reached the maximum
#> Convergence check: ✓ no problems found
#>   best start converged      yes (32 EM iterations)
#>   stage-2 starts converged  20 / 20
#>   best LL replicated        20 times
#>   LL at EM / after Newton   -9995.7125 / -9995.7125 (gain 0.0e+00; max |gradient| 1.3e-13)
#>   smallest class            0.100
#>   · EM converged; 1 Newton steps (polish = true) raised the log-likelihood by 1.0e-07 (max |gradient| 1.4e-03 → 8.4e-08); the reported solution is the Newton one
round(profilemeans(p_vv), 2)
#>          class1 class2 class3 class4
#> sleep      7.09   7.60   5.88   7.89
#> activity   3.54   5.78   2.84   0.92
#> fruitveg   2.97   4.39   2.43   1.96
#> stress     6.09   3.29  11.10   8.68
#> lonely     4.60   3.70   6.05   7.62
#> lifesat    6.99   8.26   5.19   4.63
round(profilevariances(p_vv), 2)
#>          class1 class2 class3 class4
#> sleep      0.46   0.37   0.86   1.09
#> activity   2.18   4.31   2.09   0.38
#> fruitveg   1.33   1.48   0.88   0.83
#> stress     3.34   2.25   4.74   6.09
#> lonely     0.63   0.28   1.01   0.86
#> lifesat    1.00   0.82   1.62   2.20

The profile with about six hours of sleep and stress near 11 is the “stressed short sleeper” profile; the one with almost no physical activity and the highest loneliness is the “isolated and inactive” profile (generated means: sleep 5.9 and 8.0, stress 11.0 and 8.5, loneliness 6.0 and 7.8).

Class enumeration

Fit a sequence of models and compare them. fittable() stacks their fit statistics:

fits <- lapply(1:6, function(k) lca(aces, starts_with("ace_"), K = k))
names(fits) <- paste(1:6, "classes")
fittable(fits)
#>           K    n npar        ll      aic      bic    sabic     caic   entropy
#> 1 classes 1 1500    8 -6197.364 12410.73 12453.23 12427.82 12461.23       NaN
#> 2 classes 2 1500   17 -5413.828 10861.66 10951.98 10897.98 10968.98 0.7812622
#> 3 classes 3 1500   26 -5316.153 10684.31 10822.45 10739.86 10848.45 0.7935852
#> 4 classes 4 1500   35 -5248.007 10566.01 10751.98 10640.79 10786.98 0.7593466
#> 5 classes 5 1500   44 -5240.280 10568.56 10802.34 10662.57 10846.34 0.7712432
#> 6 classes 6 1500   53 -5234.394 10574.79 10856.39 10688.02 10909.39 0.7699156
#>             smallest replicated starts
#> 1 classes 1.00000000         20     20
#> 2 classes 0.35914474         20     20
#> 3 classes 0.18180184         10     20
#> 4 classes 0.09873811         20     20
#> 5 classes 0.05216880          2     20
#> 6 classes 0.04633679          2     20

BIC has its minimum at four classes, the generating number. The Vuong-Lo-Mendell-Rubin test (lmr(), Mplus TECH11) and the bootstrap likelihood-ratio test (blrt(), Mplus TECH14) compare each model with the model with one class fewer. The bootstrap runs on the Julia threads.

lmr(fits[[4]])    # 4 against 3 classes
#> ━━ Vuong-Lo-Mendell-Rubin test: 3 vs. 4 classes ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
#>   H0 log-likelihood (K - 1 classes)  -5316.153
#>   2 × LL difference                    136.292
#>   Difference in parameters                   9
#>   VLMR p                                <0.001
#>   Adjusted LMR LRT                     134.253
#>   Adjusted LMR p                        <0.001
lmr(fits[[5]])    # 5 against 4 classes: not needed
#> ━━ Vuong-Lo-Mendell-Rubin test: 4 vs. 5 classes ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
#>   H0 log-likelihood (K - 1 classes)  -5248.007
#>   2 × LL difference                     15.454
#>   Difference in parameters                   9
#>   VLMR p                                 0.111
#>   Adjusted LMR LRT                      15.223
#>   Adjusted LMR p                         0.116
blrt(fits[[4]], reps = 100)
#> ━━ Bootstrap likelihood-ratio test: 3 vs. 4 classes ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
#>   H0 log-likelihood (K - 1 classes)  -5316.153
#>   2 × LL difference                    136.292
#>   Difference in parameters                   9
#>   Bootstrap samples                        100
#>   Bootstrap p                           <0.001

The H0 log-likelihood and the likelihood-ratio statistics agree with Mplus; the VLMR p-values follow Vuong (1989) and Lo, Mendell and Rubin (2001) as published and can differ from those printed by Mplus. Simulation evidence favours the BLRT together with BIC (Nylund, Asparouhov and Muthén 2007).

The tests can be added to the fit comparison table; the lowest information criteria are set in bold:

lmrs <- lapply(fits, function(m) if (m$info$fit$K > 1) lmr(m))
lm_table(fits, lmr = lmrs, format = "markdown")

Model fit

Model K Par. LL AIC BIC saBIC Entropy Smallest (%) LMR p
1 classes 1 8 -6197.364 12410.729 12453.234 12427.821 — — —
2 classes 2 17 -5413.828 10861.655 10951.980 10897.976 0.781 35.9 <0.001
3 classes 3 26 -5316.153 10684.307 10822.451 10739.856 0.794 18.2 <0.001
4 classes 4 35 -5248.007 10566.015 10751.977 10640.792 0.759 9.9 <0.001
5 classes 5 44 -5240.280 10568.560 10802.342 10662.566 0.771 5.2 0.116
6 classes 6 53 -5234.394 10574.788 10856.389 10688.022 0.770 4.6 0.244

LL = log-likelihood; Par. = free parameters; saBIC = sample-size adjusted BIC; Smallest = smallest class (estimated proportion).
LMR p = Lo-Mendell-Rubin adjusted LRT p-value (K - 1 vs. K classes).
Lowest information criteria in bold.

Models with the same number of classes that are nested (for example equal against profile-specific variances) are compared with compare_models(). It reports the naive likelihood-ratio test and the Satorra-Bentler scaled difference test that Mplus uses under MLR, based on the scaling correction factors (scaling_factor()):

compare_models(p_eq, p_vv)            # profile-specific variances fit much better
#> ━━ Nested model comparison ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
#>   p_eq (M0) nested in p_vv (M1)
#> 
#>   ───────────────────────────────────
#>   Model             LL  Par.  Scaling
#>   ───────────────────────────────────
#>   M0: p_eq  -10165.364    33   1.1289
#>   M1: p_vv   -9995.712    51   0.9916

#>

#>   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

compare_models(p_eq, p_vv, p_full)    # each model against the previous one
#> Nested model comparison
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Model   K  Par.          LL  Scaling        BIC  df  Chi-square      cd  Scaled chi-square  Scaled p

#> p_vv    4    51   -9995.712   0.9916  20343.720  18     339.304  0.7398            458.650    <0.001
#> p_full  4   111   -9842.132   1.1041  20451.024  60     307.161  1.1998            256.008    <0.001

#> Each model is tested against the previous one. Scaling = MLR scaling correction factor; cd = scaling correction of the difference; scaled test = Satorra-Bentler (2001; Mplus MLR).

The chi-square reference distribution does not hold for models with different numbers of classes; use lmr() or blrt() for those.

Tables

lm_table() turns models and results into tables in plain text, GitHub markdown, LaTeX (booktabs) or HTML, and can write them to a file:

lm_table(m4, what = "parameters")                       # classes side by side

cd = 0.7398 (scaling correction of the difference, Satorra-Bentler 2001); ΔBIC (M1 - M0) = -214.964.

In R Markdown or Quarto, a table is emitted as is; use the format that matches the output ("markdown" or "html" for HTML documents, "latex" for PDF). Any data frame can be formatted the same way with lm_table(df), and other packages can add methods by building an lm_tab() and rendering it with lm_render().

Satorra, A., & Bentler, P. M. (2001). A scaled difference chi-square test statistic for moment structure analysis. Psychometrika, 66(4), 507–514.

Vuong, Q. H. (1989). Likelihood ratio tests for model selection and non-nested hypotheses. Econometrica, 57(2), 307–333.
